utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom and those just outside assisting us. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, before I give an opportunity to continue to cross-examine you, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, are you ready to continuing cross-examining Mr. Flynn?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's reaching controls at times that is difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, good morning.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We were discussing yesterday the visit of Mr. Akashi to Knin on the 7th of August and for Your Honours references we're dealing with matters in P20 at page 3, just for reference. I'd like to produce a document at this stage concerning Mr. Akashi's visit. If the registrar could produce Prosecution 65 ter document 4025. This is a report of Mr. Akashi's visit that we'll be seeing on that day that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not yet in evidence I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, because I know it takes -- it's on the screen already. It takes a bit of time to upload.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You want to tender that? And it's not in evidence yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This will not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I already ask. Yes, perhaps I should allow you to finish your sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This will not be a controversial document and go straight in. All parties will be producing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we first get a number and then it will immediately be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D29, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D29 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I? I wish to request the Defence, as we move through the documents, to also refer by tab numbers because we have got binders with tabs from the Defence so I could easily follow through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Cermak Defence or is that all Defences or --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Cermak Defence, Mr. President. The numbering if you follow the list you sent, you know, the numbers against each document on our list. Thank you. If it's not possible, that is all right, Mr. President. I will follow on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it Mr. Kay will do his utmost best to see whether he can meet your needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a report of Mr. Akashi's visit. Can you see it on your screen, Mr. Flynn?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's the report to Kofi Annan in New York, and you can see there in paragraph 1, in about the sixth line, that he says that he met the new Croatian army commander for the Knin region, General Cermak. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not military governor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Where did the title "Military Governor" come from?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a usage that I fell into while I was in Knin, and I really can't say exactly where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We may be able to fill in those gaps later on. During his visit, Mr. Akashi met a number of people and also toured Knin as you told us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: His overall impression of the town of Knin is that it suffered considerable damage from artillery fire, and he gives his observations. "However, the damage to the town structures, while noticeable, was less than I anticipated." Would that accord with your observations of Knin?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He goes on to say: "Large numbers of homes and buildings were left untouched by the fighting." Would that accord with your observations?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "Utilities were still off, but General Cermak told me he expected water and electricity to be restored today and phones tomorrow." Were you aware of those failure in the public services?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of the issue in these first days of Knin after its liberation that the town had to have its services restored to normalise public life?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say I really don't recall that issue in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of the issue that we see in paragraph 2 again: "Cermak told me very soon, perhaps as early as tomorrow, regular HV units would be removed and only military and civilian police would remain together with the nascent civil administration."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Presumably in your tour with Mr. Annan, although you may not have been with him at all the meetings, you were collecting information as to the circumstances of Knin as you had arrived in it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, the reference to Mr. Annan most likely is a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. I take it that you wanted to refer to Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, although on that day it was rather difficult to get detailed information because, as I think I described in one of my reports, there was a large crowd moving around with Mr. Akashi. We were in the hospital, for example. We could barely move down the hallway, and so we certainly didn't have an opportunity or I didn't have an opportunity that day to do any significant fact gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn over the page to page 2 and look at section 3 of the report where the hospital is mentioned, on that day, on the 7th, the hospital had doctors in operation within the building working.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And within that hospital were people of Serb ethnicity as well as Croatian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware, if we turn to paragraph 4, of the meeting between General Cermak and Mr. Akashi at the camp in which they -- or Mr. Akashi handed over a copy of the Akashi Croatian government agreement that we looked at yesterday?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that's Exhibit D28. Again the concerns in that meeting was for assistance that Mr. Cermak could give concerning the people within the camp which the UN had temporary control or custody of because they were within their area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The issue at that stage as well was whether those Serbian people who'd lived under the Republika Srpska Krajina flag in the region, whether they were going to commit themselves and stay within the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was a great unknown and something that the UN and the agencies such as yours needed help to solve as a problem.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, that would accord with the relationship between the UN and the Croatian government as defined by that Akashi agreement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you present at that meeting between Mr. Akashi and Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware, maybe from other sources, about the assurances Mr. Cermak had given in relation to the safety and security of Serbian people who wanted to stay?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe I was aware of the assurances that had been given at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you become of that -- aware of that later on, at subsequent meetings or subsequent exchanges?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it would be fair to say that right from the start that that was one of the objectives expressed by Mr. Cermak to the UN of the desire he had to help people stay within the Knin region who had lived there previously?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a statement he made on a number of occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Again in paragraph 4, there is five lines, four lines from the bottom the issue of freedom of movement because the UNCRO troops by that stage, on the 7th of August, had been kept within -- those that were there, within the UNCRO compound.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I missed the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. On the 7th of August, at that time in the visit of Mr. Akashi, the UN authorities were concerned about their own freedom of movement because the Croatian forces had, so to speak, kept them within the UNCRO compound?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware on that day, the 7th of August, that in fact Mr. Cermak had only arrived the day before?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall being aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The issue in paragraph 5 concerning --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we scroll down just a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The issue in paragraph 5 concerning the interviews of military-age men in the UNCRO compound to be interviewed by the Croatian authorities, that is a matter again that arises within the Akashi agreement, our Exhibit D28?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The terms and process as to how such interviews would take place as to identifying whether any people within that camp were war criminals was a matter that still had to be ironed out as between the UN and the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were aware that that was a matter of concern for the UN and something that further negotiations were needed upon?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning now to page 3 of the report by Mr. Akashi, paragraph 6, third line: "In his tour --"

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's just a little small to read right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. In his tour Mr. Akashi makes this comment: "The most striking aspect of my conversations however was the fact that all of those with whom I spoke uniformly expressed a desire to leave Croatia."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're asking if that's what the report says?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, the report says that. Does that accord with your experience as well on that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say uniformly. I recall that some individuals wanted to go back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the vast majority, in fact, had made their minds up to go either to Republika Srpska or in Bosnia or Serbia proper?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The great majority had, I would say, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Within the UNCRO compound as well were you aware of the fact that there were Croatian -- people of Croatian descent within that camp at the same time? It wasn't just people who were from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or people who were Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One clarifying question, Mr. Flynn. The question was put to you whether the vast majority had made up their mind to go either to Republika Srpska or in Bosnia or Serbia proper, and you said yes, the great majority had. Now, to go there, would that -- did you understand that to be the wish to go there and stay there or to go there at least for that moment and then further consider and decide whether to stay out of Knin or to come back to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding was that at that point the majority of people in the camp wished to leave the area and go to these other locations mainly for their security. I did not understand that they wished at that moment and had decided at that moment to emigrate or permanently leave Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To settle there. That's -- yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document I want to turn to arises from a series of questions that you were asked about yesterday arising from that first HRAT report of the 8th of August, Exhibit P29. We have no need to call that up. Concerning the numbers that were dead, and it was a question that I believe came from the Bench yesterday. Could we please bring up Prosecution Exhibit 65 ter 850.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not in evidence yet. It needs a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see that document there? That's now in English and the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While zooming in takes place, Mr. Registrar, this would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this becomes Exhibit D30, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Mahindaratne, can you say already something about whether you object?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may have a minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll hear from you. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a report from a man called Brigadier Dr. Brkic, and he was the chief of the health administration, and he filed a report on hygiene and sanitation measures taken in the period from the 5th to 12th of August, 1995, and you can see this report was sent to the Croatian chief of staff. On the 5th of August it says that he came to Knin on that day to carry out an inspection, "... which I perform in every event of this kind and I encountered the following situation..." and he gives human sanitation and technical measures about bodies in the area and you can see information about what he found. On page 2 of this document, on about the eighth line, you'll see mention of an order he made to Mr. Ivan Delic, engineer, to deal with the bodies in conformity with the Geneva Convention and carry out complete forensics examination. And the report goes on to deal with steps taken by him. You gave evidence yesterday about a meeting that happened on the 7th of August that you thought Mr. Cermak had mentioned details about 61 people being buried, and within that passage it mentioned 70 centimetres apart. Do you think that that conversation in fact could have been with someone with more technical expertise such as this man Dr. Brigadier Brkic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that question. The witness is being asked to speculate on a matter I don't know if the witness is familiar with, and the witness has not even indicated that he's familiar with this documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, he -- it's put now to the witness that certain people have more technical knowledge. He's asked whether he -- whether he considers it's a possibility that he had spoken. He's not asked to think about the content but just about to whom he had been speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That doesn't need any technical knowledge apart from that it needs the skill perhaps to distinguish between knowledgeable and less knowledgeable people in this field. So therefore the objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see the point of the question. The passage you referred to yesterday, you weren't precise. You didn't say General Cermak said this. It was, "Well, maybe my recollection," "It could be," "I think," and I'm just pointing out that in that paragraph it mentions that 70 centimetres as some sort of gap which I presume is an international standard, and it seems that there was a man on the ground here who has an expertise in this. Do you think in fact it could be the case that this information arose from someone else rather than General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. He was often -- he was always accompanied by others, and it's quite possible he was accompanied by this individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I wonder if this could be admitted as an exhibit now as D30 because it's a document from the Prosecution and uncontroversial I'd have thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I don't know whether the whole collection of Prosecution documents are all uncontroversial, if that was the case, Mr. Kay, there would be no need to ever object to them, isn't it? That would be the logical consequence of that. But, Ms. Mahindaratne, is there any objection against this?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Exhibit D30 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you meet this man Brigadier Brkic who was in charge of dealing with the dead and the sanitation of the terrain and was in Knin throughout this period?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He may have been at the meeting at which I was present on the 8th of August with General Cermak, but I really don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Did you know the people who were with General Cermak in your dealings? You haven't given us many names in your testimony, but certainly him as the front of house, were you aware of the other people who may have been with him or who had other responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I referred earlier to two other individuals who I recall were usually with the general, and unfortunately I can't recall their names with certainty. I remember what they looked like. I described them in my statement. I can describe them again for you if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No need, because I am going to ask you about that. It is material. General Cermak didn't speak in English. He spoke in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He spoke through an interpreter who was a Croatian army liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did the UN also have an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When dealing with General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So at these meetings you had two interpreters?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But do you know where your interpreter came from?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a number of different interpreters over the course of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't want their names or anything like that as I appreciate that can be sensitive, but were they from an official system or were they other people who were, shall I put it this way, around in the region?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. They were all on staff. They were UN staff members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were they local people?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were local, yeah. The majority, the great majority were local.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We're aware of the situation as we've had other evidence in the case, and I don't want to go into backgrounds. You described someone as being a deputy to Mr. Cermak, and you described him with a small goatee beard. Did he speak English?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I wouldn't say a goatee beard. It was more of a full beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were there in fact two interpreters, as you recall?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he wasn't an interpreter. There was a third individual who did often serve as interpreter, a gentleman with rather long grey hair, a long beard. I remember him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The one with the beard you've described as the deputy who spoke some English, he was a Croatian army liaison officer, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that with certainty because I'm not exactly sure what you mean by Croatian army liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of the structure that had been developed between the UN and the Croatian government where there was a liaison system? There was a whole hierarchy coming down from Brigadier Plestina, who was in Zagreb. I don't know whether you met him.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But he was the chief of this particular hierarchy, and then moving down on the ground into Knin where there were two liaison officers who worked with UNCRO liaising with General Cermak and UNCRO. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I wasn't aware of the formal structure per se, but it was evident to me that there were members of the Croatian contingent there who were responsible for liaison and who conducted liaison and who in fact were very competent at liaison, and that would certainly include this individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Would it be fair to say that his English was not perfect? It was not a fluent English?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a fair statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. He picked up the language. That would be fair to say, but he did not have a technical skill?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't comment on where he got it or how he got it, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I just use that as a characterisation from officially trained people that we have here to those who speak a bit of the language.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would just say he wasn't fluent --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but I never had any serious understanding difficulties with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. This is the man you describe as the deputy?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. Can we look now at a document, Prosecution 65 ter 1623, which is the appointment of Mr. Cermak to his position and why he was in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I take it that that would be D31?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's correct. This becomes Exhibit D31, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you inform us as soon as you see the document whether there's any objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I know this document, Mr. President. No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D31 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The series of questions I'm asking you is relevant to the issue of the deputy as well as the title that you gave Mr. Cermak about military governor, Mr. Flynn. You can see the translation of the document here?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a decision from Zagreb on the 5th of August, 1995, by the president, and it says: "I hereby appoint Colonel-General in the reserve Ivan Cermak to the post of commander of Knin garrison HQ."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then it says: "I hereby release Major Marko Gojevic from Kijevo of his duty as commander of Knin garrison HQ and appoint him to the post of the deputy commander of Knin garrison HQ."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, did you know that in fact Mr. Cermak, until he was appointed this day on the 5th of August, was actually a civilian before this appointment and working in civilian life?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did know that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he'd been working there for a number of years having left politics and his previous roles in relation to the government?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know at that time that he was taken from that civilian life and arrived in Knin in this position on the 6th of August? He came straight into it.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know how much time, how recently or long before he had been appointed to this position, but I knew that relatively recently he had been in civilian life, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we see his appointment on the 5th of August, which coincides with the completion of Operation Storm, and you know that he was there on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From this document you'll see that the previous holder of this position, commander of Knin garrison HQ, was previously a major, Major Gojevic.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he in fact was downgraded from that position and put to the post of deputy to the commander?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that that's what this document says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And Marko Gojevic, did you know him by name as the deputy to Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. And when I referred to deputy before, I really meant deputy with a small D, if you will. I didn't mean that the individual we discussed earlier to my understanding was formally deputy in rank to General Cermak in Knin. I meant essentially his close assistant or advisor. And in point of fact, he was also the individual who was there and who received us if General Cermak was not available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Is he the individual to whom you reported what had happened at Grubori on that evening of the 25th of August at 4.30?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just not sure, but I doubt it frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Well, for the record, and this may help you to remember, the individual that you're talking about with the beard who spoke a bit of English and was a Croatian army liaison officer with the UN was someone called Dondo.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that name, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's the man you're talking about when you use this name Juric in your statement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And his first name Carolj Dondo.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Now, of importance here in the document that we're looking at, D31, is the fact that you see the actual appointment of Mr. Cermak to the post as commander of Knin garrison HQ and not military governor.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I evidently was not aware of his formal title.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. Were you aware, in fact, that there is no role of military governor within the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. There is a role of military governor within certain circumstances as we're aware. After the Iraq conflict there was an appointment by the American forces of a military governor.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to look at the position now of what a -- a garrison commander, as he was appointed, does, what their function is, because in your statement you recollect -- you gave your belief, your thoughts, and I don't criticize you for that because you quite properly -- you put that description with what you were saying, belief, thoughts, as to General Cermak's role. All right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter number 3408. And in this document we will need to turn to page 21. It is quite a full document, and it's the is service regulations of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, dated the 20th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D32, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you tell us already whether there is any objection to this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D32 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 21, please, of the regulations. I can see it. You'll see here what a garrison is described as. A garrison is an area in or near a populated place where a company or higher units of the armed forces are housed.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, could it be magnified just a bit, please. Thank you. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Presumably you don't need the Croatian part on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't speak or read Croatian. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. I don't know whether it's possible for the witness to move it so that he just has the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, there are two elements involved here, what the witness can read on his screen and what the public will see, the public --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- might be interested to follow these proceedings and then of course if we would limit it to English only, we would exclude a large portion of the population in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's okay. I can read it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm getting to grips with a new courtroom for me and what can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you can see there what the garrison is in paragraph 50. You can see how he's appointed. In fact, he should be appointed by the orders of the Main Staff. And you can see in 52 that the garrison commander is responsible for billeting, order, discipline and service. All units and institutions within are subordinate to the garrison commander as regards issues of order, discipline, and service. And at the entrance to the facilities where the command is located, you put up a sign, and he has responsibilities to issue rules on order, discipline, supervision of behaviour. So that's rules of behaviour of military persons in the garrison. Page 22 --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that now. It needs to be scrolled down, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You can see that there are these various rules --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, now -- okay. Here we go. 22, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 22, defining the billetings, training ranges, bathings in rivers, summer or winter uniforms. 55, instructions for the behaviour of units and institutions within the garrison in case of readiness, natural disasters. Reception and billeting in 56. 57, military ceremonies. And the command may define the organisation and work of technical sanitary construction, and other services. So these are from the rules. We're just going to look at a series of documents now. There are many more, but just to put it into context as to his role so that I can ask you a question, and I think you know what the question is that -- that's coming.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can pull up Prosecution 65 ter 2907. This is not an exhibit yet and is headed "Setting Up of Garrisons," dated the 16th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D33, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne, could you give us already --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then D33 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The document here we're looking at as you can see on page 1 is the setting up of garrisons, and 16th of February, 1993. And you agree a regulation, in fact, issued before the Croatian republic had control over Knin and the occupied territories?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we go to page 4 of this document, which on the previous pages has a various number of garrisons such as Benkovac, other places, Dubrovnik, Sinj, Split, Zadar, as to the areas they cover. And there you can see in Knin garrison it's the territories specified there, Knin, Nadvoda, Kistanje, Ervenik, Otric , Kijevo from where Major Gojevic came and Civljani?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that regulation says that it's in Gospic until it moves to Knin.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And someone within the Home Guard battalion had to carry out tasks although they weren't in Knin?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we go to page 6, paragraph 2 there, or number 2. The commanders of the garrisons are directly subordinated to the commanders of the military districts. And in 3, the commands of the garrisons of the navy, air force, and defence are in charge of preparing, organising, and setting them up.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And paragraph 5 on the next page, page 7. All other questions relating to the setting up of garrisons are to be dealt with by the commands of the military districts. If we go through this document to page 9, we see a report on troop numbers for Knin garrison headquarters.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 31st of August. And this is an official form filled in on that day, and it says: "Five active officers, one drafted private, three civilians, and overall nine."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Manned for wartime duty, active 2. Let's go to page 10. And we see here again various numbers relating to the break-up of the unit: Who is active, two; reserve, two; non-commissioned officers, four; privates, two; civilians, ten. There it's signed by a lance corporal Juric, but I suspect that wasn't you were dealing with, this is --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I make that point just to deal with it. So a small unit within the garrison HQ. And did that accord, in fact, with your dealings with General Cermak? When you went to his HQ, he had a number of civilians there and a small unit of people with him.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the headquarters of General Cermak there were certainly not a lot of personnel present ever, and I had the impression that General Cermak had responsibility for a larger number of people, and he certainly let on to us that he could have an influence, for example, over the presence or removal of Croatian military units from Knin. I never believed that General Cermak had direct command responsibility over those units, but my impression was that he considered that he might be able to influence or not -- or to influence the removal or not of those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I put it to you yesterday that he was there to help the UN, and that was -- would be -- that would accord, that kind of function, with helping the UN, because that was a desire of the UN, wasn't it, in trying to deal with the aftermath of the war within that area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, General Cermak was our -- certainly my main contact, most senior contact, and he was virtually always cooperative and certainly generally encouraging about the possibility of helping us with some of our requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say he's a positive man?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was fairly positive with us, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware that he'd had a successful career in business pre-establishment of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he was successful in business when Croatia was established?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not exactly sure of the timeline, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you were aware that he had those qualities?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that he was a successful business man, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware that he had had an interest in the early days of the Croatian state in helping organise logistics?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As a specific field.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we look at page 11 and we see the 26th of September, 1995, a further report on this establishment, and it reads the same. Overall nine we see on that page. And on page 12, a lesser number of people, in fact. The handwritten signature at the bottom has got Assistant Commander Marko Gojes, but that would be Marko Gojevic. Looking at that headquarters, what actually was there, you entered the building and he had offices on the first floor. You go up some steps and there were offices on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The UN also had a liaison officer within those officers working with the Croatian army liaison officers?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually I don't exactly recall that, but that's certainly true, I imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It wouldn't have been unusual.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Down on the ground floor of the garrison HQ was a large public kitchen that was eventually established.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember as you go in through the front door you go up some steps, there's a big dining-room. To the left there was a big kitchen, a mess hall -- the mess hall on the front and a big kitchen, and outside a big feeding area as well where everyone went?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sounds familiar, but I don't think I paid a lot of attention to that premises in particular, especially when we were there. Our objective was to meet immediately with the senior authority there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that within the garrison HQ there were many people milling around? There were civilians. There were members of the public. It was a busy terminus.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just can't really comment on that. I just don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it too long ago to --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just don't recall a large number of people milling around, but there may have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's all right. You just tell us your recollections. That's very, very fair. I want to now go to Prosecution Exhibit -- sorry, not exhibit, 65 ter number 785, called the organisational order regarding work, order, and discipline at garrison HQs. And this is an order from the 27th of August 1993 from the Ministry of Defence and, Your Honour, could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D34, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit D34 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This document is an organisational order regarding work, order, and discipline, and it notes, you will see in the first two lines, not all HQ commands have been set up. And order number 1: "The commanders of the military districts, navy, air force, anti-aircraft defence are superior and responsible for the entire work, order and discipline in the garrison HQ in their areas ..." Turning to page 2, paragraph 2 of Exhibit D34. "The garrison HQ commands do not have an operational function and the right to issue orders to Croatian army units except precisely prescribed authorities regarding work, order and discipline at the garrison HQ outside of barracks and other military facilities, within the tasks provided by the Rules of Service of the Armed Forces."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that lack of operational function actually accords with your impression of General Cermak from the observations you made about five minutes ago in answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I said earlier that I was not entirely clear on his operational authority. I did not understand General Cermak to have direct command authority over the large part of military units in Knin. But as I say, he gave us, gave me, the impression that he had the ability to influence the presence or removal of military and police units in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. Paragraph 3: "The garrison headquarters' commands are required to establish cooperation and coordination of tasks of the garrison HQ with administrations and departments for defence, departments for care, stationary telecommunications, information systems, departments of the military -- of the Ministry of Defence headquarters, administrations and other bodies and institutions of the Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Interior, and other government administration organs."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just looking at that paragraph, the words "cooperation and coordination of tasks," were you aware of General Cermak's role in trying to get the electricity, sanitation, water, public utilities working within Knin?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to those specific responsibilities, no, I don't think I was aware of his responsibility in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Mr. Kay, your question was about his role. That could be his -- and that's apparently how the witness understood the question, what his responsibilities are, but you have of course a factual role and a structure of responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we clarify that the witness also has no knowledge, at least that's what I understand, about a factual role he may have played, whether or not strictly within his responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I -- I have no particular knowledge of that. I mean, I think that there may be some connection with these issues, for example, and questions about the general welfare of the civilian population in the area, and I know that General Cermak, for example, addressed the question of rehabilitation of residential structures. He appeared to be directly responsible for individuals who were temporarily housed in the local school and what might happen to them. So with regard to those sorts of humanitarian issues he certainly seemed to have a direct responsibility. But with regard, for example, to the restoration of utilities and that sort of issue, I don't recall knowing of his responsibilities there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you again used the word "responsibility." Do you exclude for the possibility that he addressed these matters even if it would not be within his formal competence, within his formal responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He well may have. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. Could we always try to make perfectly clear when we're talking about roles whether it was the formal role as described in whatever kind of documents, and sometimes a role which might go beyond what the formal responsibilities were. Both directions. Go beyond or not taking responsibilities where there are formal responsibilities. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, we don't need to deal with that in fact, and we don't need to deal with paragraph 5. Attached to this, if we go to page 3, is "Instructions on regulating some issues within the jurisdiction of garrison headquarters." And this document, which was attached to the one we're looking at, contains various functions that have to be done. For instance, if we look at 2(b), garrison headquarters with several barracks and units. The ZM commander shall compile a list of staff on duty and their assistants. All sorts of organisational objects here. Turning to page 4. I don't say it in a light-hearted manner, but "Arrangements for swimming in rivers, seas or lakes." This shows the scope of various functions. Paragraph 4, "Employing military police units." The commander is required to arrange a procedure with the closest unit of the military police and have them intervene in the case of unrest, accidents, et cetera, when an MP unit is indispensable to establish order and discipline in the area of the garrison HQ, and arrange temporary employment of MP patrols to supervise work, discipline and conduct of military personnel in public places. We'll look further at that in a moment in relation to another order. And number 5, which comes from that last series of questions I asked you. "The ZM is required to establish cooperation and coordination with the public administration or the police stations in the area of the ZM, and in conjunction with the arrangement and reciprocal exchange of information regarding maintenance of work, order and discipline and the conduct of military personnel in public." "Cooperation and coordination with the police administration or police stations." I want you to particularly note that because it does not say subordination. And do you appreciate, Mr. Flynn, the difference between being in control of a police and actually cooperating and coordinating with them?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And why I ask this question is because from the terms of your statement that has been put in evidence, D20 and D -- P20 and P21 exhibits, it was your impression that Mr. Cermak had control of the police?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say -- I don't think I ever said he was directly in control --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I would say that this description that you are offering presupposes, in my view, a fairly orderly environment, and certainly in August of 1995 many of these matters were almost irrelevant, because the whole zone was in complete disarray and -- and essentially was lawless, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We had a situation where a state had regained control of its own territory. The Republic of Croatia had for the first time occupied this area that was part of its territory. Its mandate and writ had never extended there before. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To say it was territory probably doesn't accurately define the extent of the region. We're talking about a very big region, in fact, aren't we, when we look at the boundaries of what was called Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the area formally known as Sector South?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And after the successful military campaign, the State of Croatia had to try and organ take control for its administration over this territory?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was a scene of chaos.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say more lawless. Chaos implies that there was a lot going on. This, as you know, was a very sparsely populated area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there was a general sense, especially in the early days, of a lack of control, including a lack of police control, and that's why your reference to coordination with police stations is a little unrealistic in those early days, because there were no police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One was opened up in Knin on the 6th of August by the Minister of the Interior Jarnjak.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Knin, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that was filmed -- were you there when it was opened?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But it was a public event that was -- have you seen film of it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. But you're aware of the fact?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That there was a police station?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We'll be looking at that later on. Page 5, section 7, "Organising food and accommodation of non-permanent military personnel," dealing with billeting, accommodation, catering facilities, security of military facilities. I'm going through this rapidly because I know that the learned Judges will be able to read this. It's not because I'm skipping information. I hope you understand that, Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Page 6, section 12, firefighting, fire prevention. Again, various emergency provisions, although oath-taking I wouldn't include in that. 16: "Setting up garrison headquarters detention units." A barracks detention unit. And page 7, lay down instructions in section 17 on order, discipline and supervision of the conduct of military personnel at the ZM. Then again we have further issues to do with control and we have no need to go into further details because I know the Court will be able to read this document for themselves. Next document I want you to look at, because it arises from those provisions within that framework, is a document 2D010001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D35, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an exhibit that has not been produced by the Prosecution through its 65 ter regime, nor in Mr. Theunens' expert report which the Court has had filed, but is a document we can look at concerning the control of the military police as issued on the 6th of July, 1994, by the minister of defence, Mr. Susak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne, could you give us already your --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can't seem to trace this document amongst the documents we've got notice of from the Defence, but we were informed this morning that there will be a couple of new documents being tendered in evidence. I haven't had time to go through this document. May have a couple of minutes, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from you. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's at tab 107.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we're looking at this, Mr. Flynn, because it's relevant to that passage concerning the military police within the instructions to the garrison HQ.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's important that we give a complete picture. I'll read the text: "... with a view to removing any ambiguities in the system of command and control over units of the military police and with regard to the information about the failure to respect the system in the area of responsibility of the 72nd [Realtime transcript read in error "77th"] Battalion of the military police in connection with military police platoons in Croatian army brigades on the southern front I hereby order." In that preamble were you aware that the 72nd Battalion of the military police was in fact in this district of the Split Military District within the area of Knin?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said to us you didn't pay much attention to units and what their particular pedigree was.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I paid attention to which branch of service, let's say, individuals belonged to. For example, whether they were police or military, but within those I did not personally note as a rule the specific unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To you it was just military police rather than where they came from.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 1 makes all units of the military police to be subordinated to the military police administration under the command and control of the chief of the military police administration under rules from the government. Were you aware that the chief of the military police administration was a man called Mate Lausic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may just point out, I think the transcript records the 72nd Military Police Battalion in two places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to the Prosecution. I actually can't see the transcript from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Then this is now put on the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And I have no objections to this document going in, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then D35 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So in your position within HRAT you had no dealings with the chief of military police?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you have liked to have seen him and set up some kind of coordination project with him?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We really considered that dealing with General Cermak was adequate to our purposes of informing the authorities of issues that were of concern to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it gives here various powers to the chief of the military police administration as to his authorisation to commanders of military police battalions.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should say also that I assumed that other components of the UN presence in Knin were dealing with other elements of the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And what about in Zagreb, which is really where the headquarters of most institutions were.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I'm sure that was true as well. That's one reason that we sent our reports to Zagreb, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was going to ask you that later on. Let's just deal with that now because you raise it. Your reports went to which office in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went to something called the Humanitarian Crisis Cell, which was, I believe, part of the office of the SRSG at UNCRO headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And we can see here that the essential thrust of the whole of this order is that the military police are subordinated to the military police administration. It can be looked at in detail later on. Paragraph 9 on page 2, decisions on manning the active force of military police battalions at the proposal of the battalion commander in agreement with the commander of the military district, other institutions, shall rest with the chief of the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Number 10, which is very important for the issues I've been raising before: "All orders regulating the system of command of military police units or manning of military police units in a manner contrary to the Rules of the Organisation and Work of the Military Police of the Republic of Croatia and to this order shall cease to be in effect." So that the terms of this order keep control of the military police within the power of the chief of military police.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that in fact revokes that order that we were looking at concerning the military police in the garrison regulations. Remember that paragraph I showed you about the military police within the garrison HQ?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne and Mr. Kay -- Ms. Mahindaratne, you said Mr. Kay could check that on the transcript. You said, "I think the transcript records the 72nd Military Police Battalion." I saw as a matter of fact that it was the 77th Military Police Battalion where it should have been the 72nd. That's I take it that you wanted not to refer to what was on the record but what should be on the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. I wanted to point out that instead of 72nd it was recorded as 77th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes and that does not clearly appear on page 36, line 13, but now we have all confusion dealt with. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just about to go to a new topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps it would be better to -- to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, could you give us any indication as to how much time you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We are doing very well. I had in my mind at the start that I would be about five hours, because obviously this is an important witness for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I had to amend my papers last night to try and assist the Court in relation to questions that had been made from Your Honour Judge Gwaunza concerning the reports of crimes on the 7th of September, so I've endeavoured to increase it slightly. I hope to inform the Court how long that section will take. I haven't had quite time to work that out, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you start saying that you're doing quite well, then we expect some new reduced number of hours. You have said five hours. What is your estimate approximately now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think my original estimate was right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at how far we've gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course we are dealing here with quite an extensive 92 ter statement for which even the Prosecution took three additional hours. So could I ask other Defence counsel -- first of all, I don't know to what extent you're aware of what Mr. Kay is exactly dealing with, but, Mr. Misetic, what is your expectation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order we've agreed upon is that counsel for General Markac will go after Mr. Kay and then the Gotovina Defence. You're absolutely right, it depends on the materials Mr. Kay will cover but as of right now I would say approximately two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mikulicic -- or Mr. -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll be conducting the cross of Mr. Flynn and I estimate at this point, depending on what comes in, no more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that brings us to -- we have now had approximately two and a half hours, I think. Yesterday, was it one hour? Mr. Registrar, could you -- you gave me the information before court, but I think it was close to one hour. One and a half hour, now two and a half. So another four and a half to five hours to go. That's -- yes. That means that, Mr. Flynn, we have still a good expectation that you could leave before the weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be appreciated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Until now cross-examination has taken -- yes. I was a bit overoptimistic. I'll check the numbers later. We'll have a break now. We'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we turn to 2D01-0009. We're going to look at a series of newspaper reports now, Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, for a minute. May I just have an indication as to the tab number, please, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And these deal with Mr. Cermak's job and what he said at the time. The first article is only on our screens at the moment in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it could be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have it in English as well on the left side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. This is a translation by the Defence, Your Honour, and a document produced by us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I take it -- I make one observation here. I noted that some of the documents that were earlier introduced into evidence, the translation was marked as unrevised. Could you please -- these were documents provided by the Prosecution, although tendered by the Defence. Could the parties see that we do not have any dubious translations? I'm not saying that if they're unrevised that they're not good, but of course they still need to be revised, and the Chamber would like to avoid that we have major -- especially if we are talking about these core documents as were produced this morning, that at least for those documents that we have proper translations. So could you please perhaps together seek that these important documents are revised and that we have final translations of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I tender this into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is this part of a series and is it the whole of the series or is it document by document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's going to be three documents. We'll do it document by document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that will be number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D36, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the link is so tenuous. This is a press article. I don't know what is the basis to have this admitted in evidence through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would prefer that it would be tendered from the bar table or --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I withdraw -- I do not object, but I just wanted to place on record how I do not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it's admitted into evidence, and it goes without saying that if something is published in a newspaper, it's not for the full hundred per cent sure that it would reflect what someone said or that it reflects what has happened. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: D36, Exhibit D36, it's simply a very straightforward report, Mr. Flynn, on matters we were talking about this morning concerning the appointment of Mr. Cermak as the commander of the Knin garrison, which was in the public media.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And exactly the same as the order we looked at this morning about Gojevic as the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And a brief resume of Mr. Cermak's positions in the last five years.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And those are facts that we -- we've already covered, and I've just put this into evidence to say that his position was of a publicly appointed nature. You had a UN press department run by a man called Mr. Roberts within your circle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he produce articles from the publications of Croatia for you so that you could learn what was happening?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a press service within the UN. I'm not sure if Mr. Roberts himself was responsible for that. There was a lot going on in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: All right. Did you see this article or a translation of it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now move to, in fact, a press article produced by the Prosecution on their 65 ter list, 4422.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tab 17.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D37, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do the Prosecution object to it going into evidence? It's on their list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D37 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is an article dated the 10th of August, 1995. Headline: "We must catch the remaining rebels." And it's an interview with General Cermak about the restoration of Knin and the surrounding area. We can see what's written. I'd like to go to line four: "The newly appointed commander of the Knin garrison HQ Colonel-General Ivan Cermak was confronted with the complex task of coordinating the military and civil police, the UNCRO forces, the European Union peace mediators, in a town without any living conditions, and where there is still a small number of fanatics ..." Again from your observations of his task, what he did, is that an accurate small picture of his role coordinating between the institutions?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say so, and I'd like to say that it was primarily his responsibility as described here for coordinating military and civilian police which was of interest to us with regard to the security situation. I think you have shown that a garrison commander has a number of tasks and duties including some of rather mundane nature, but it was certainly his responsibility with regard to the re-establishment of security that was of particular relevance to our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we look at the third paragraph, which is a question that's asked, and this is an answer: "We are in the process of restoring the Knin garrison. We are doing our best to bring normality back to a town with no civilian authorities, no water, electricity or telephone lines. On Monday we withdrew Croatian army units from town, deployed them in positions around Knin; the town now has members of the military and civilian police, whose complex job is to bring life back to normal and to keep law and order."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: An accurate assessment, would you agree, of what was needed on the 10th of August, 1995, in Knin?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It goes into further detail on page 2. I'm just going to look at the second paragraph. Other matters can be looked at in more detail. Of the second paragraph: "I have spoken to Serbian refugees who are housed in UNCRO's reception camp and many of them want to live in the Croatian republic. They are aware that they made a mistake ..." and then it goes into further detail, ending with: "They had not heard about President Tudjman's missive and lived in great fear ..." and then it mentioned propaganda.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Some did want to live in Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that many of them had lived all their lives in Croatia and that was where their property was, and so certainly a large number did want to live in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On page 2, if we look at the bottom paragraph which begins: "Not only do we not have any problems with the peacekeepers, we collaborate extremely well. I have talked to Mr. Akashi and the commanders of UNCRO forces, and we soon found a common language to our mutual satisfaction, so we have agreed on particular aspects of cooperation." Would it be right to say, in fact, there was a cordial relationship between the UN and General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general I would agree with that, although certainly at times General Forand, for example, took a tough tone in his meetings with General Cermak because he was frustrated with what he saw as a continuing lack of security. So some of the meetings were rather tense in that regard, but fundamentally there was certainly a sense of cordiality, if you will, and mutual respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. This was a series of problems that the UN was bringing to General Cermak, but he was dealing with them politely. He wasn't being aggressive towards you. You may have disagreed with what was happening, but on the personal, one-to-one level, this was a respectable relationship between you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
