utterances.text: I think so, although I do think there was also, at least in what was said, an evident difference in perception of what was taking place. Now, I don't know if that reflected true beliefs, but sometimes I think our concern for serious lack of security was not fully shared by the general, at least in what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have two sides here, don't we, in the sense of the UN, the Croatian government, and a person from the Croatian state in Knin at that time? You would expect, would you not, for him not to disbelieve his own government or his own people in the same way that you would not disbelieve your UN hierarchy? That's a fair comment, isn't it, in relation to your jobs?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I would expect the general to be very careful, certainly, in conceding possibly any wrongdoing or misconduct on the part of the government or agents of the government that he represented, but there were some times in which I felt that plainly evident facts were disputed by the general, such as the wide scale of burning that was taking place in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. In relation to that relationship, the position adopted by him was, by and large, to present the Croatian point of view; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. But there were occasions when in fact he didn't, and he -- he conceded or he said, "No, there is problems, and we must sort it out"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And there were occasions when incidents were brought to his attention. You used the phrase in your evidence that he said he would order something to be done.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's that word "order" that I want to look at, because what he said would have been, "I will speak to the civil police. I will tell the military police." Not order, but saying that he would pass on through information that which you had mentioned. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't think that I put down incorrectly what was said. I think there may have been some inexactitude on the part of the general about actions he would take and perhaps regarding his actual authority, because when I used the word "order" I didn't use it lightly, and General Cermak did carry himself with a sense that he had a certain authority. But as I said yesterday, I was not and still am not exactly sure of what his actual authority was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's apparent from your evidence. And you were, of course, talking through interpreters.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we just go to page 3 of this newspaper report, and it's the last two sentences. "... we hope that thanks to continual coordinated and successful action of Croatian army and police force we will arrest them." That means terrorists, in fact. "After that we shouldn't encounter any great problems in the course of restoring civilian rule, reviving and repairing the town."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly what you mean by terrorists?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It comes -- I'm not actually interested in that part and it's a fault of the over-highlighting. I'm actually concerned with the last sentence, Mr. Flynn. It's his function or his job, what he was doing, being involved in restoring civilian rule, reviving and repairing the town, being concentrated upon Knin.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, although he did as, you know, also take a very direct role, for example, in the negotiations regarding the displaced persons in the UN compound who were to be interviewed. Now, whether that is directly related to restoring civilian rule or not is perhaps an open question, but there were some areas that perhaps went somewhat beyond strictly restoring normality to a community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was the point I put to you concerning helping the UN as a -- one of his jobs that he was doing. His door was always open to you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he was available, either him or someone, in his office for you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, this is repetitious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This has been answered these questions about the openness and always even without short notice. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are about to leave this document I would like know because I would like to seek clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am leaving this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, both on the first page and perhaps we could go back to that, we find a reference to -- and I'll try to read slowly: "Are there still any armed rebel Serbs in Knin who did not surrender when the Croatian army entered?" And then in the answer: "We find that there are still many Serbs -- rebel Serbs in town, but you can't see them during the day, but during the night they behave like common criminals, slyly ambushing our police force. There are still quite a few of them." This seems to be referring to the same what we found on the last page, that is that people should be arrested. Does this correspond with what you at that time learned about terrorist attacks as it's even mentioned on the first page by Serb rebels attacking the Croatian police? Is that -- does it fit in the information you received at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't recall that that was the situation, Your Honour, after about the 6th of August. From the UN side I don't think that there was a sense that there were rebel Serbs in the town, for example, who were actively targeting Croatian units. After a couple of weeks it became evident that there were some holdout members of the RSK army who were in the hills and more or less in hiding, and I don't exclude that there may have been a number of attacks of small scale they might have been involved with, but certainly in the town itself there was no sense that there were still rebel Serbs who were posing a threat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Next if we can produce 65 ter number 530, tab 11. This is a newspaper article of the next day, the 11th of August, 1995, an interview with General Cermak, and its detail can be looked at on another occasion, but I just want to ask about the first paragraph, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D38, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne, could you already --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Exhibit D38 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This article here, we can see on the sixth line the question is asked of Mr. Cermak: "Dr. Tudjman has appointed you commander of the Knin garrison. What are your tasks and jobs in the conditions of the immediate aftermath of the liberation of Knin?" So the question in fact that I've been asking you this morning.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The reply is: "My task is to coordinate the establishment of the civil authority and the running of all systems necessary for a normal life of the town. That includes coordinating the work of the civilian police, the military police, and civilian authority. Currently, there is no civilian authority in Knin. The government has appointed its commissioner, Petar Pasic, who will start creating the civilian organisation of government on the territory of the former municipality on Wednesday."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That then was a contemporaneous description by him of his tasks and jobs. From your dealings with him, would you agree with -- with that observation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although it doesn't mention in his comments the -- the matter of the persons in the UN compound, but of course that's mentioned earlier in that article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. I'm going now to a new matter and it concerns the role of the police, starting first of all with Cedo Romanic, who was the chief of police for Kotar Knin area. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for reference purposes this is from the statement P20, page 10, line 20, and page 12, line 4 onwards to assist the Court in a cross-reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in your statement you made several observations about Mr. Romanic. I would like to turn first of all, to deal with this through documents, to 65 ter number 1687, tab 31. This is the appointment of Mr. Romanic as chief of the Kotar Knin police on the 5th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D39, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. D39 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Cedo Romanic. You knew his first name, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is his appointment, chief of the Knin district police administration. In fact, from the 5th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just a minor matter: In your first statement you may recollect that you said that you believed that he came slightly after you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Probably a mistake.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we can see there the personal details, and also the name of the minister who appointed him, Mr. Jarnjak. Again this makes it apparent that he has come from the MUP within the Sibenik police administration.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document I would like to see is 65 ter 2431, tab 69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D40, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D40 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This just needs a little introduction. The document that the Prosecution were putting on the 65 ter arises from an inquiry by the Defence, and obviously it was released by the government to the OTP. We turn to page 2 where information is given concerning the police stations which were set up in the liberated area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you can see Kotar Knin police administration, and Knin police station were set up on the 6th of August, 1995, being the day before you arrived.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although I'm not sure what "set up" would mean exactly. Obviously there's a big difference between an administrative formality and actually becoming operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You visited the actual police station in Knin?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember the date of your first visit?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't. It must have been within the first week I was there, but I just can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. In terms of the set-up of that police station, would it be right to -- to bear in mind when you first got there it would be early days of its establishment?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's say you went there within the first week. Would it be fair to say that it was not well equipped?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That it was a basic building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many police cars did they have?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would hate to venture a guess, because I couldn't know what -- which cars were parked there, which might have been out, but what was notable is that away from the police station it was very rare to see a police vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And you were aware of a problem here that they had taken control of a previously occupied area and had to set up this kind of institution?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see on this document the dates of other police stations being opened up, on the 5th of August, and 8th of August, Drnis, Obrovac, Benkovac, Gracac, Korenica, Donji Lapac, Donji Srb. Did you visit those police stations?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I must say I would tend to take this information with a grain of salt as we say in English. For example, we couldn't go to Benkovac until more than a week after that date, and if there was a police station there I'm surprised the UN wasn't even permitted access to the town. So I find these dates a little hard to believe, again in terms of any operational capacity, even a pretty minimal operational capacity for some of these towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which was the problem that was faced generally with -- with the events that had happened?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, I think that's a fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. If we go to the next document, which is 2D01-0011, tab 115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D41, Your Honours, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you have the document on your list?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D41 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 4th of August. It comes from the MUP, the assistant minister of whom was a man called Josko Moric. Did you know Josko Moric?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have any dealings with the senior police officers?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Knin you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Generally in Croatia. How far up did you go in relation to your contacts?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, really only to the local chief. We didn't go any higher within the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. The local chief being Mr. Romanic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think we had dealings in the -- in the second and third week of August, I believe, with -- I think there was a police chief in Korenica, if I recall, and in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Those other police stations that we've looked at in -- in the list.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which you said were probably set up later.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have dealings at all with a police officer called Cetina?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who would have been Romanic's superior?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. I'm dealing with the aspect of your testimony concerning the role of the police and what they were -- were doing, which is why we're looking at these documents. This is dated on the 4th of August, 1995. It is to all police administrations as we can see on page 1, and we can see the terms of why this was issued, and it's a series of orders concerning the organisation to be adopted by all police administrations effective for Operation Storm. That would be right, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we can see the concerns and the orders made. Paragraph 3, step up security and monitoring of the crossing of the border. Step up monitoring of vehicles, passengers in vehicles, and inspect vehicles. And then in 6, an order that puts that into the context of Operation Storm because it concerns the attacks that were obviously happening on that -- that day. So that's a document about preparation. Can we turn to 65 ter number 4553 -- 4534, sorry. 4534. Tab 101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D42, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D42 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 7th of August, 1995. Subject, assistance the Zadar Knin police administration. For the needs of a rapid terrain clearance of the town Knin, urgently mobilise 100 civilian protection conscripts from the area of Sinj. The unit shall be dispatched for jobs relating to the clearing of the terrain and roads in the area of Knin. And signed by an assistant minister, which is a document that shows that the MUP could take steps to increase police strength or assistance if they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge of that. I don't know what their actual capacity was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, but on the face of this order it seems that this assistant minister was ordering that rapidly and urgently that 100 conscripts go to the area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in fact it was a concern of yours about the failure of the police to order more policemen to the area, and that's apparent from your statement.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, or to actually effectively ensure that more police showed up. We weren't, needless to say, concerned about the order or not, but I was concerned with what we saw on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. You appreciated that you were dealing with a state that ran on a hierarchical system, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And at the top somewhere someone would have to order extra policemen who would have to come to the region?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the document that Mr. Kay is referring to is not the document that's on the screen. I'm finding it difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's the one I've got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What -- I have on my screen a document, although it's difficult to see because it's not zoomed in, the 5th of August, 1995 with the letterhead Republic of Croatia, Ministry of the Interior. That's what I have on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is the same but I thought Mr. Kay referred to a document dated 7th August, which is what is on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check on the transcript. Could you give us line and page where the 7th of August appears?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I did Your Honour, because I put my gaze on to another similar order and it's my mistake, and the Prosecution is quite right. There were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that although it appears that the substance and content might be approximately the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that you are talking about two different documents and this document is of the 5th of August, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And it's my mistake. The substance is very similar. Dispatch 100 personnel and the Zagreb PU another 100 personnel to Zadar Knin police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the MUP was aware of the need for policemen in the area, certainly on this date, the 5th of August. That's right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we look at 4553, tab 103 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D43, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D43 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'll deal with this quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One hundred civil protection conscripts, which was the document I was wrongly looking at before. So again support from the top being given to this region by the Ministry of Interior so it would seem?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's just coming up on my screen. I'm not sure I really understand what "rapid terrain clearance" means here, the clearing of the terrain and roads in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that is, you know, removal of debris or if it could mean clearing of the terrorists who were alleged to be there, I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whatever --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It seems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, it seems that in the original it is ciscenje, the language, which has given rise in many cases before this Tribunal through a thorough investigation on what that actually means. Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. I was just reading the first sentence does not say ciscenje. It says asanacija. It is in the second sentence though, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the second sentence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We've got the documents there and I've got no need to dwell on it too much. Let's go to the next section of documents which concern cooperation between the MUP and the military police. So 65 ter 2206, tab 71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D44, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D44 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're looking at this because of your concern in the statement about not having sufficient forces and not having sufficient control in this area and we'll look at this document first of all which is from the military police administration, 3rd of August. We can see the 72nd Military Police Battalion Split as well as other battalions, and its subject: "Activities of the military police, cooperation, joint activities of the civilian and military police, obligations of the military police towards the arrested paramilitary and militia members." And we can see a series of orders emanating from the 3rd of August, a working meeting between the MUP has been held. The tactics and method of the MUP -- of the military police and the civilian police in the beginning of the attacks in the newly liberated areas were agreed according to the conclusions in order to implement them on all levels of command in the army. And we can go through quickly on page 2. This order makes the police administrations and commanders of police stations bodies to which the military police must contact immediately on all levels of command, set up check-points, follow the progress the army, jointly patrol to ensure public order and peace in towns, and other duties. Page 3 concerns paramilitaries and how people are to be taken to reception centres, questioning, and how people are to be dealt with. And on page 4 we see it emanates from Major General Lausic. So this seems, certainly at the beginning, that there was a plan by the military police to coordinate with the MUP in relation to security in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay, are you asking the witness about whether he observed anything, or are you asking the witness to interpret what this document says, where it then would need a foundation why he is the person who should do that and why not, for example, the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suppose I'm guilty of taking this quickly and at speed because of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand but even within the time allocated to you, you should still follow the rules. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, and it's a very good -- good ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your dealings with the civil police, were you aware that the Knin police administration had, in fact, obligations, as well as the military police having obligations, to coordinate and work together?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were a whole series of -- of orders, nothing to do with the Zborno Mjesto of Knin, General Cermak that had been issued relating to the duties and obligations of the military police and the civilian police to work together to provide peace and security?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find this very surprising, because well into my stay there there seemed to be, as I say, a minimal police presence, and we repeatedly and earnestly brought this to the attention of the authorities including General Cermak and Police Chief Romanic, because I felt that there was a serious deficiency in security in the area. So it's quite remarkable to see these orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were unaware of the orders --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- that I'm about to look at with you, and it's relevant to your opinion and beliefs and thoughts at the time, which is why I'm bringing them to your attention. You didn't know the background behind the military police or the civil police in terms of what they had to do?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew what their responsibilities were, but I didn't know their duties pursuant to these orders that you -- that you showed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's pre-Storm on the 3rd of August, and we're going to look further down -- down the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we'd bring up 65 ter 431, tab 99. Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A number should be assigned. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D45, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D45 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This arises from that last question I asked you. It's dated the 4th of August. It comes from the military police administration whose chief was General Lausic. It's the records of a meeting they'd had on the 3rd of August with the Assistant Minister of the Interior Josko Moric. We've seen an order from him already today. Mr. Djurica, chief of police sector. Mr. Nadj [phoen], chief of crime. Colonel Gugic, chief of the ministry of defence information and security service administration. And if we look at page 2, it's delivered to regular military police department, crime military police department, traffic department. Page 3, on the 4th of August, sets out the working meeting of those leaders of those departments, and its topic was coordination of activities of MUP, military police, intelligence services in the period of preparation and during the planned offensive actions of the Croatian army in the following period. And if we turn to page 4 --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, when you say MUP that means civilian police?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Ministry of Interior. It's become a common phrase in this court here --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- well, all courts here. Yes. I'm sorry. And we can see on page 4, Mr. Moric, the assistant minister of the ministry of interior, the MUP, pointed out the fundamental principles of the operation of the police and military police in the state of war based on their experiences. Major General Mate Lausic, head of the military police are aware of negative experiences. They have to ensure full cooperation and absolute carrying out of tasks from the scope of their activities. Page 5. I'm just taking passages as this can be read at length later on. In the second paragraph Major General Lausic said about the meeting of the highest officials had among others render the military police and the MUP responsible for complete efficiency in carrying out tasks during combat activities of the Croatian army; pointed out that the commanders of HV units were warned that they would be personally responsible for the discipline of their subordinates, otherwise not even a much larger number of the military police force would be able to ensure -- secure discipline. This report goes on and I don't have time to deal with all of those factors, but it comes down to this arrangement they had for cooperating in providing security in the area at the highest level?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would it be possible to scroll down just a bit --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on the English version? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which page are you on?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's okay. The Court has done that. And is there a page after this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, there are other pages.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And there are nine pages, in fact, and I've distilled the essence of it. Anyone can correct me if I'm wrong, but --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just trying to see the extent to which it addressed in particular the post-combat situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We will get to that, in fact.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because what I'm putting to you are a series of measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the witness wants to read the document in its entirety, I think it's fair to let him if the witness is going to be questioned on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any wish on your part to read the document as a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe not at this moment, Your Honour, but perhaps I would request to do so depending on the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps -- yes. Okay. Then perhaps -- sometimes it saves time if there is any problem of context that the witness is allowed to read the document during the break and that then questions will be put to him. So please proceed, but if there's at any moment you feel the need that you need to know more about the context of what was read to you, please tell us so that we can take appropriate measures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's just a simple point that arises and why I'm using this document, is there was this structure, nothing to do with General Cermak, between the MUP and the military police as to their responsibilities and obligations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object to that, Mr. President. The witness is being asked to give an interpretation to a document, and I don't know whether there is a basis for that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it is not even a question. It is an observation by Mr. Kay why he addresses this document. So I'm waiting for his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it was going to be this:

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of that at the time in your dealings with Cedo Romanic, for example?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of these documents and these orders that you have shown me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. The reason why I'm showing them is because of your thoughts that Mr. Cermak somehow controlled Cedo Romanic so that he was within his hierarchy or some connection, and that's why I'm showing you these documents which you weren't aware of at the time, but you've given your thoughts and beliefs.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My main impression was that the relationship there related to resources for the most part, that General Cermak could play a role with regard to the resources that were put at the disposal of the police forces, but I was not certain of General Cermak's capacity in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. I'm going to move now quickly to 65 ter 2299, tab 73.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D46 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you already ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D46 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kay, I must confess to you that the issue just raised by Ms. Mahindaratne, the context of the document, reading the whole of the document is keeping me busy behind my screens here. Going through certain elements of a document where the whole of the document is in evidence creates some puzzles now and then. Just to give you an example, the 3rd of August document you referred to earlier, that is the pre-Operation Storm document, apart from the parts you referred to I also read, for example, at paragraph 3 that women, children, and elderly people from the liberated areas should be handed over by the MP members to the closest police station, and then it follows that they have to be registered. That is -- it doesn't say anything about being arrested. Nevertheless, apparently groups of the population, of which one would wonder why they have to be handed over to police, that leaves a puzzle which might be worthwhile to address at any moment either by the Prosecution or the Defence. And also since they have to be registered there, whether there are any such registers, whether this Chamber would find people of all ethnicities on those registers or a specific ethnicity. That's -- this raises quite a lot of questions. Therefore, reading the whole of the document, I tried to do it at the same time listening to your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, please accept, and the Bench, my apologies. I know it's a tough task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm just telling you what goes through my mind, because sometimes it may help the parties to know what approximately comes to the mind of the Bench so that they can probably respond to that or pay attention to it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There are many documents, Mr. Flynn, and I have taken a few to provide a little picture of each of these sections that I'm dealing with in terms of your evidence --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- and as I have put to you what the facts were concerning General Cermak, which is my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So we're looking at this letter dated the 10th of August, 1995, from the Military Police Chief General Lausic, and it says: "According to reports from the field and in particular the territories from --" sorry, Assistant Minister Moric, my mistake, to General Lausic. "According to reports from the field, and in particular the territories of Lika-Senj and Zadar-Knin police administrations," with which we are concerned, "... cases are being noted of individual Croatian army members on liberated territory stealing movable property, burning houses and killing cattle that strays around the area." So a problem which reflects the matters you've raised in your evidence. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "In addition, there is a lack of cooperation at check-points, roadblocks between the police and the military police. "We understand the size and nature of the tasks that you have to contend with, we kindly ask you to take measures to eliminate these things." So a significant letter from the assistant minister in relation to ongoing problems on the 10th of August that had been brought to his attention from the police administration.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is significant. You're of course not asking me to comment on the reliability of every statement in that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, the reference to individual Croatian army members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That would be something as a given that you would take issue with from the terms of your evidence. But what I'm asking you about it is -- is this, that there again behind Cedo Romanic in the hierarchy of the civil police, the assistant minister writing to the chief of the military police saying what are you going to do about these problems that we're facing?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Something that you were unaware of in the background and unaware of when you made your statement in 1998?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was unaware of this letter, yes, and that sort of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, and this won't -- this is a fact. There is a selection of documents here to give this convenient picture relating to your testimony, and there are a few more on this subject I want to turn to as they advance in time. 65 ter 1133.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tab 67.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D47, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D47 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The previous document we looked at, as you quite rightly pointed out, you would disagree with the characterisation in that report of individual cases.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But it would seem that that's what had been put up the chain from the police station level to the assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not -- I can't say that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Unless he characterised it like that and that's another option.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're looking now at the document from the military police administration, again dated the 14th of August. We can see the 72nd Battalion of the Split Military Police. It's subject is the implementation of military and police tasks in the zones of responsibility of the military police units. It's an order. It's post-Operation Storm order as you can in the first paragraph. And then point 1 concerning combat readiness. No need to tarry there, but page 2. In paragraph 3: "I will leave it to the commanders of the military police units to decide when they will completely abolish their forward command post." It deals with zones of responsibility in paragraph 5 and 6. Let's go to 7. Third line: "... commanders of the military police shall start to analyse check-points in their zones of responsibility, and in line with the assessment and together with the MUP, police station commanders, police administration chiefs, they shall set up joint check-points which will work energetically to prevent unauthorised entry. They shall check and search cars to prevent uncontrolled and unauthorised removal of 'war booty' from the newly liberated areas." At page 3 is a series of orders concerning check-points, and in paragraph 11 the duty to provide as requested by the commander of the 72nd the necessary assistance with forces and equipment to carry out military and police tasks in the newly liberated area, as well as in Split and Sibenik. So again behind what you were dealing with, there appears to have been a hierarchy in which the problems you were concerned with on the face of it were being addressed at the highest level.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This documentation all looks perfectly in order, but of course on the ground there was nothing like this sort of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly. And that's my point to you about Mr. Cermak's role, because this is completely outside his domain. There is a separate hierarchy that you were unfamiliar with which had the responsibility to deal with these issues of concern?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, but again there were occasions in which General Cermak made representations to us about communicating concerns to Zagreb. As I say, on one or two occasions his comments were translated to me as ordering increased police presence, although in reviewing my notes I also saw that in early September at one point he made a comment about requesting strengthened forces, police forces, from Zagreb. So -- and I also would reiterate that Mr. Romanic appeared to think that some of the resources available to him depended to some extent on General Cermak. But it's quite right that there is an extensive amount of paperwork here that would indicate another forum in which these issues were being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that's the point of these questions, Mr. Flynn, concerning your statement and your assessment in 1998 involving Mr. Cermak. You were unaware of all this information.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And what this document shows, that certainly on the face of it, in paragraph 11, that the -- another battalion of the military police has the duty to provide support to the battalion that was in the Knin area, the 72nd, with the necessary assistance, that the issues concerning provision of support that you were concerned with were -- were being put down to a particular commander and he was told to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what these documents indicate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And the next document 65 ter number 2391, 17th of August, tab 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar. Yes, I drew the attention of the registrar to something else at this very moment, so I'm guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D48, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Yes. D48 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You quite rightly, Mr. Flynn, pointed out that you would take exception with the individual cases and this letter here on the 17th of August of Mr. Moric at the Ministry of Interior to the military police commander, the chief Mr. Lausic, indicates that there are great problems in this area that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may just observe this document we're talking about is labelled top secret so of course there was really no way I would have known about this document at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And that's a fair point in relation to your state of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "It is apparent from reports submitted by police stations and police administrations that cases of houses being burned down and other people's property being stolen are recorded on a daily basis in the territory liberated in the Storm operation. Perpetrators of these acts in most cases are wearing Croatian army uniforms. Our information points to these persons who are formally and in effect members of the Croatian army but that there are problems over those who are not and are abusing the uniform. I hope you will understand the problems that the civilian police faces, which is legally bound to protect life and property. I therefore conclude that the joint work of the military and civilian police in this area has not produced up to now results in accordance with the basic provisions of our state policies and legal system and that it needs to be changed. We need a new method in order to eliminate these problems."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just ask, this is from whom and to whom again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is from the assistant minister Josko Moric.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the interior?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of the interior. Who is in charge of the civil police. All right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To the man in charge of the military police, General Lausic. So at the highest levels on an operational level, we've been looking at a series of documents between these two.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Above them are the ministers.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But it's these two in the paperwork. And they know their work has been a failure from the terms of this letter.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. So again Mr. Cermak is not a person to whom this problem is being referred to at that level. You would agree?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, although I do believe there was a reference to a certain role of coordination between military and civilian police, but no, certainly, I wouldn't attribute to General Cermak a leading role in dealing with these kinds of issues when assistant ministers, if that's what they are, are exchanging correspondence on this issue. Of course they have to base their findings on information they get from the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm sure that General Cermak would have played a role in that as others presumably would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the field of speculation whether someone would have played a role in something. And, Mr. Kay, it appears clearly that this correspondence is not addressed to or coming from Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever that means is a different matter, but I think it's not very useful to -- I mean, that's so perfectly clear that we don't have to pay a lot of attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I'm just looking at this document now on the 18th of August, 65 ter 644, tab 85.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D49, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D49 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again I'm producing this because of your perception of Mr. Romanic and his role, which in your statement made him in a way look powerless, but here we have a document dated the 18th of August from the Ministry of the Interior, the assistant minister Josko Moric. We can look at his signature at the end of this document. To the police administrations, and you'll see Zadar -Knin.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you'll see on page 2 that it goes to the chief at Knin. So we go to the superior police administration down to the police station at Knin. And Mr. Moric in this order says: "Written and oral reports by police stations and police administrations shows that these are daily cases of torching of houses, illegal taking away of people's movable property ... "Most acts perpetrated by individuals wearing Croatian army uniforms. The facts indicate that these individuals are, formally and actually, members of the Croatian army, but there are individuals who are not ... who are wrongfully wearing Croatian uniforms. "Torching of houses and taking of property assumed such proportions that it is inflicting political damage on the Republic of Croatia both in the country and abroad. "In order to put a stop to this problem, I hereby issue the following order." So this order was going to Mr. Romanic, page 3. "Police administration chiefs must immediately convene a meeting with commanders of military police, battalions, to inform them of the problem and of the decision to put a stop to it. The meeting must be informed of the decision about those crimes and put a stop to it as of today." When you look at that paragraph 2, this needs further examination. "The meeting must be informed of the decision that cases of torching of housing and illegal taking away of people's movable property that have hitherto occurred will not be operatively investigated, but a stop must be put to cases of this type as of today." Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That they weren't going to investigate according to the assistant minister those crimes until this date of the 18th of August with which you have been concerned?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find that rather inexplicable, and I certainly wasn't aware of that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would also point out that there were a number of killings that occurred before the 18th of August, and certainly those would have required investigation if nothing else. I'm not sure if they are referred to in this document or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. But that's a very fair observation. Paragraph 3 about check-points being mixed between civilian and military. Paragraph 4: "It should be agreed as of today an on-site investigation and forensic and operative processing will be conducted after every case of torching of houses and taking property. "If the military police can't do it the civilian police will do it alone, irrespective of whether the perpetrator wears a Croatian army uniform or not. "Commanders of military police battalions are to be requested to inform, through the line command, commanders at the lower levels of responsibility of this order. "Police administration chiefs shall relay this order to commanders of all police stations and branch police stations and immediately send reports."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Is this an order given by Mr. Moric also to military police or only to civilian police?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Only to civilian police on the pages.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, at the last question the witness put, and I ask you, as a matter of fact, to interpret this document which comes a bit of a surprise, but it exactly deals with the same matter, the same question I had, and I'm not inviting you to tell us what -- how we have to understand this document but, rather, how the Defence understands this document so that we know at least what your position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In 1 and 2, police administration chiefs, that are civilian police administrations I do understand, must immediately convene a meeting with the commanders of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 2 it says: "The meeting must be informed," I cannot understand that in any way and else by those who are ordered to organise such a meeting, "of the decision," unclear by whom, "that cases of torching of houses and illegal taking away of people's movable property that have hitherto occurred will not be operatively investigated." Now, therefore, that's how I understand this document at this moment, civilian police commanders have to convene a meeting with military police commanders to inform them about what has happened, and also to inform them that any of these acts that hitherto occurred will not be operatively investigated. Does that mean that the civilian police tells the military police, "We're not going to do it"? Or are they saying, "Whether by you or by us, we'll leave it behind us. We just look to the future and will not investigate what has been done"? Therefore, I fully understood the question of the witness, and I'd like know the position of the Defence how you understand especially these paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not inviting you at this moment to start arguments, but in order to follow your line of questioning and to better understand the evidence that you're presenting, it might be interesting for us to know how you interpret these two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was happening here was that there was a complete hierarchy working entirely on its own without Mr. Cermak on both the police -- military police side, civilian police side at their highest level, that the responsibility for the failures of those particular bodies, military police and the civilian police, was not a responsibility of General Cermak. This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, that's not an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether -- I just want to know whether he, the civilian police, is sent to inform and to instruct the military police as well not to investigate, or whether you say, no, this is just an instruction for the civilian police not to investigate and to inform the military police of the non-investigation. I'm not talking at this moment in any way about the role and involvement of Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I misunderstood the question. It's very difficult for the Cermak Defence team to see what was behind this particular order and why it was issued. It looks as though it was some form of general amnesty that the assistant minister was giving in relation to these particular crimes as the witness in my view observed, and that he was saying to his police chiefs, "This has to stop now. You have no need to operatively investigate those particular crimes. Inform the police administration of this decision." That's how I interpret it. And you'll see in paragraph 3 that it's a request to the military police to form mixed check-points, and that they should, in paragraph 4, agree between them. So it looks to me entirely as though the assistant minister is attempting to get the civil police and the military police to work together and to combine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To jointly desist from further investigations of what happened in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good to know what the position of your Defence. If any of the other counsel, of course, would like to at a later stage explain their positions, that is appreciated, because it's unfair to ask Mr. Kay how he interprets this and not to ask other Defence counsel. So if there's any wish to do so in the near future, please let me know. Mr. Kay, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have one more document in this sequence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we deal with that and then have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- and then I turn to something else. 65 ter 2976, tab 49. If it could be given a D number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D50, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit D50 is admitted into evidence. Before you put a question to the witness, Mr. Flynn, I just would like to know whether the matter I raised whether that was -- whether I understood your question well as that it was this specific point was unclear to you as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, it's clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As I've said, Mr. Flynn, I've taken just a selection of documents to deal with these points. This is the last in this sequence. It's from the 22nd of August. You can see it's from the Ministry of Interior, deputy minister. That's Mr. Moric. From the MUP. It goes to the police administrations. You can see Knin. To the chief personally. And on page 2, "In our telegram cited above, we ordered linking with the military police in order to stop houses being burnt and property taken. We sent a letter to the military police administration." That's to the General Lausic, the chief, "In which way describe the magnitude and significance of this issue. As a result, the military police administration has sent an order to all military police battalions ordering them to link with the police administrations to solve the problem." It refers to the crimes, not including murders, and then it asks to be monitored and to be informed of the cooperation, in paragraph 1, between the police and military police, to describe that cooperation in section 2, whether there are still some incidents of these particular crimes, who were the perpetrators, about on-site investigations, how many of them, on page 3, are crimes being investigated, how many perpetrators of crimes have been identified.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, I think it goes without saying you were unaware of Mr. Romanic's obligation to his hierarchy in relation to these particular steps.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see that this letter also is marked top secret, so I don't think he could even have told me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. And therein lies the issue of your assessment of Mr. Romanic's role and what he was doing. Would you agree you weren't in possession of all the facts?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if -- if in -- it may still be that in -- in a way he was unfortunately powerless, but I certainly was not aware of this activity which was taking place behind the scenes, and he did seem to have the active input of his ministry on ways to deal with the problem -- problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But from your assessment his ministry didn't send him any extra police or any extra resources.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in significant numbers, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know at all what resources were available to the Croatian government at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Or what resources in terms of hardware, vehicles, radios?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wasn't aware of the details on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did it look to you as to whether the local police were well equipped or poorly equipped, or give your own characterisation.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say poorly equipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you. I have no further questions on that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break. We will resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn, an area concerning the civil police I want to ask you about. Did you know that they were responsible for the collection centres? And by that I don't mean the UNCRO compound but the collection centres like in Knin where people were taken.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what you mean. You mean responsible in terms of security or in terms of running the centres?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Running them, that it was part of their duties.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have been, but offhand, no, I don't really recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recall recollect visiting Mr. Romanic to get permission to go into the Knin detention centre at the school, collection centre?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may well have been. I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And there were -- you went to the collection centre, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And they were civil police officers who were in attendance there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's quickly look at 65 ter 420, tab 83.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit D51, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D51 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is dated the 4th of August. It again comes from Mr. Moric, the assistant minister of the interior. It goes to the military police people as well as, down at the bottom, for the attention of police administration chiefs, and its subject is collection centres. And it says on page 2: "In order to execute the tasks of Operation Povratak," that means return, "all indicated police administrations must immediately undertake the following preparations." And it gives a scheme for the layout of a collection centre, how they're to be looked after, the admission and procedure. Page 3, previous intelligence and criminal processing. And it goes for information on page 4 to the military police administration. So it seems that those collection centres by order were the responsibility of the local police.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And we can see that in the next document 2D010029. This isn't in the Prosecution's tabbed bundle but has been hand-delivered because it was a document released today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D52, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do the Prosecution have any --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just take a minute and I will let you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile that gives me an opportunity to ask one additional question. The last question put to you, Mr. Flynn, was: "So it seems that those collection centres by order were the responsibility of the local police." Nevertheless, we see that instructions are given not by local authorities but by higher up authorities. Did you draw the conclusion on the basis of the document, or did you answer the question with in the back of your mind other information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course the document does indicate that some aspects of those collection centres are under military police authority related to the processing of -- of persons suspected of direct involvement in the conflict, and -- I'm trying to recall. There was some discussion about our access to -- to the people in the school and possibly also General Cermak's role in that. But with respect to my answer to the previous question, I was basing it on the document which indicated that -- that, generally speaking, it was the civilian police that had the authority over those collection centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the question was local police, not civilian police. That's exactly what I'm -- that's at least what I read on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if a letter is sent from a ministry which is not a local authority --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and gives instructions to how to deal with matters on a local level, then whether it's a local responsibility or a central responsibility is still to be -- well, at least you could argue that if local authorities receive instructions for a higher up level that it's a shared responsibility or primary responsibility from the higher-up authorities or that the authority's left to the local police. That's -- these are all different interpretations of what you could understand from a correspondence between a central authority and a local authority. So therefore I wondered whether it was your conclusion on the basis of this document or whether there was anything else that you had in mind when you said that you would agree that it was a local responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was nothing else, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document dated the 7th -- the next document dated the 7th of August, 1995, may fill in some gaps on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You can see it's a letter from the chief of administration. Ivo Cipci from the Zadar-Knin police administration collection centre report and it encloses the lists of person in the collection centre in Knin which was sent to Sinj as a notification and sent for information to the Ministry of the Interior amongst others. If we turn to page 1 --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President. I'm not certain as to what Mr. Kay is referring to as the next document. We have -- we have the previous document on the screen and I have no objections to the admission of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem is he referred to a document, I think, of the 7th of August where, at least in the document which is on my screen at this moment, it says question mark August, but I take it you are referring to this document from the 10th police station coded VII, very urgent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can see what's happened. There's a front page that's been missed off in the scanning system and we can attend to that. These things have to be filed electronically, as you know, and sometimes these things happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The cover page, does that give any specific information or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's been put in as the last page and it's in fact the cover page. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's dated the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's just how the document arose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You see it now, Ms. Mahindaratne, that apparently the reference to the next document was the document I just referred to and that the last page gives a date whereas the first page does not. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And here we see a list of the Knin collection centre report. "We hereby send you a list of persons in the Knin collection centre in Knin," and then we have a list of names by commander - and there are 91 names - Commander Marko Bjelobrk, and then page 6 has the cover letter. And why it's produced here is because there were a number of people in this collection centre in Knin. That's right, isn't it, which was the local school?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This gives information on that date. Would you say that the number was about right, 91 or so people?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You, of course, came out of the UNCRO compound a couple of days after the 7th of August. Your first visit into Knin was a few days later; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. On the 9th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. On that date did you visit the collection centre in Knin at the school?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I'm not sure that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. It would have been very soon after that date, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you went to see Mr. Romanic to go and get access to the school?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That finishes that particular subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question if you're talking about numbers. Were you aware of the reasons why these people were in this collection centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm really not sure, Your Honour. I -- of course I prefer not to speculate. I know that many people ended up in the UN compound because of their fear for security. I'm not sure if others ended up in the school for a similar reason. I'm not sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm not sure of the people who ended up in the school at that early date. I know that a few weeks later we actually requested that the authorities make more room available at the school because the UN compound was full, completely full of displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But here we're talking about the 7th of August. That's the day on which you arrived.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I'm not sure exactly how or why those people ended up in the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because I earlier saw a document that women, elderly, and I think children had to be taken to collection centres, whereas just having a first glance at the document there appear to be among those apparently present or registered there we find elderly -- elderly women as well and -- not all of them, but a considerable number of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And some men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Therefore I said some of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to avoid whatever confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the population, why they were there, did you have any further information about that in these early stages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're turning now to specific --
