utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're turning now to specific roles concerning the chief of police, Mr. Romanic. Can we bring up 65 ter 1500. Tab 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And while the registrar is doing that, D52, Ms. Mahindaratne, have you --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.text: It was an overnight job, and it arose as a result of a question from the Bench yesterday which brought something to my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it, nevertheless, Ms. Mahindaratne, that you ever taken sufficient time to make up your mind.

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D53, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware that in fact the civil police and the military -- and the UNCRO police, UNCIVPOL, which is the phrase that was given to them, had a joint programme as well to work together?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that that was a standard operating procedure of UNCIVPOL really wherever they were, that they had a mandate, among other things, to work jointly with the local police. I don't think that happened in Sector South or the former Sector South for quite a period of time, and I'm not familiar with this document you're showing me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. And I -- because I was going to ask you about the time. As this document is undated, it's not one of mine. It comes through disclosure by the Prosecution. It doesn't have a date, but we'll take into account what you say about cooperation coming further down after some time. Shall we just look at it in terms of what it says? It's the rules of the joint work of the police, the MUP, and CIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see that in the former north and south sectors UNCIVPOL members will be enabled to control the work and conduct of Ministry of Interior members with respect to the protection of human rights and freedoms.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that the word "control" there means monitor essentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think so. I mean, I'm sure they had no mandate to control the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There will be an opportunity for us to ask another witness about that. Paragraph 2, the chief of the Knin district police administration Mr. Cedo Romanic and the chief of the Glina district police administration shall be appointed to coordinate the work between MUP and UNCIVPOL. And in paragraph 3, UNCIVPOL will designate officers who will coordinate joint activities on a daily basis and contact Mr. Romanic and the other person.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Coordination meetings shall be held once a week, minutes taken. Problems at can't be solved on the level cited at 3 will be resolved by UNCIVPOL together with police department chiefs of the Zadar-Knin police administration, and the people are named, and minutes taken. And then if problems exceed that level, the UNCIVPOL force commander or his deputy or the chief of the MUP police sector, Mr. Franjo -- and it's actually Durica it begins with a D that name --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- or a person whom he designates shall be authorised to resolve them. And then in 7, taking up your comment, UNCIVPOL members can observe and follow the work of MUP employees, record but without sound and video or photographs. 8: UNCIVPOL members shall be engaged to have access to police documents, certain police documents only with knowledge and approval. UNCIVPOL shall be enabled to carry out patrol activities with MUP employees and then a plan in relation to how that should happen.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to put into any time just to help us at this stage when the cooperation between UNCIVPOL and the local police was put into effect?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite some time after my arrival on the 7th of August. As I say, there wasn't, as far as I could see, a significant Croatian civilian police presence in the areas outside of Knin, and I do remember a report that I prepared I think about the last week of August that referred to a joint CIVPOL and Croatian police patrol in which the Croatian police actually withdrew shortly after entering, I think, the Plavno Valley because they were concerned they didn't have enough fuel in their car. And I think I noted that instance of joint patrolling because it was an important event in terms of what we were hoping to see. But I also know that earlier on certainly there was a professional cooperation along the lines of this agreement between UNCIVPOL and the Croatian civilian police in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And with the chief of police, but of course I'm not the best person to comment on the details of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. UNCIVPOL were part of your HRAT monitoring; is that right? You combined with the various organisations when you went out on the road?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the film we saw yesterday, that would have been with a member from UNCIVPOL, you as HRAT, and then any other agencies as part of the team?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Essentially UNCIVPOL tasked an officer or a couple of officers on a daily basis in principle to join HRAT.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. And your recollection is right concerning the documents you saw about the Croatian police not proceeding further because of fuel concerns.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One of the documents that was produced yesterday, I can't remember which one, it may be around the 4th of September.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we look at Prosecution Exhibit 31. Tab 117 for the Prosecution. And this is one of the documents produced through your evidence yesterday. It's your report dated the 10th of August.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we go to page 2, freedom of movement, and it there refers to a meeting between you and Mr. Romanic concerning freedom of movement for you being extended to Obrovac, Benkovac, and Plitvice, but on main roads.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So your freedom of movement for that particular area was not anything that came through Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. There were other instances in which Mr. Cermak informed us of increased freedom of movement. If I recall correctly, I think I may have described that in one or two reports as an order that had come from General Cermak regarding freedom of movement, but I'm not sure now that General Cermak was ordering matters related to freedom of movement. He may have been informing us on behalf of the Croatian authorities that freedom of movement had been extended to certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We can look at that later on, but you're exactly right about passes issued for the area. Did you have a pass for the area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't have passes, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have an order or something that you were able to show at a check-point?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I believe as -- as the UN we didn't need that, and we weren't testing the limits of the freedom of movement that the authorities told us we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Next document we want to look at is again one of your documents. It's P46. Tab 4 for the Prosecution. And it's your report of the 23rd of August.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure this is my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. It's one you produced, but it was signed by Maria Teresa Mauro. I think I'm looking at a different document. 3463, 65 ter 3463. I thought it was P46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have for P46 I have a different -- I have a propusnica on page 4 and the report is 10th of August --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that's what I have at least under P46.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is my mistake in looking at the table because we didn't have descriptions of the documents and I've obviously got a number confused with the court-designated exhibit number. I wonder if we could be helped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the -- Mr. Registrar, you could help us out with the 65 ter number given by Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I show 65 ter number 03463 being marked for identification as P46.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Oh, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have a problem with my -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I've got a misfiling. I wonder if anyone can help in relation with the HRAT report of 23rd of August. Oh, P47. Thank you very much. P47.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's look at the right report then. Signed by Maria Teresa Mauro. No, at the bottom it's just her authentication signature. Was this one written by -- by you? It's from Mr. Al-Alfi, but did you write the report or --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I did, but I don't see -- all I see is the cover page right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Ah, no. There's another one of 23rd of August. Sorry, Your Honour. It's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There's a P46 is 65 ter number 3463. That's the Human Rights Action Team report of 22nd August, and P47 is 65 ter number 3467. That's the Human Rights Action Team report of 23rd August. I think Mr. Kay is referring to P47, 3467.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have for P47 I have a three-page document, first page starting with "Most immediate," and then the second page as we see it now on our screen having "Note for the file."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry. I've got another document of the same date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Than would be number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'll give the ERN number just in case anyone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has difficulties in finding it on the basis of ERN numbers but if you give the ERN number then most likely Mr. Registrar will be able to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 00351685. I hate to say it, it's got three ERN numbers on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the body language of Mr. Registrar I understand that he can't retrieve it. Could you please move on for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May we go back to this matter as it's actually a very pertinent matter and one that requires your attention, Mr. Flynn after I'm sorted out later on. You referred in your statement to Mr. Pasic, and you gave your view as to how long he'd been appointed and where he came from. I just want to look at some quick documents in relation to him. The first one --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did I say he was the Civil Defence coordinator?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The mayor.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, the mayor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D54, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D54 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's just the uncertainties in your statement about Mr. Pasic that I'm dealing with, because I think you can see from here he was appointed --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- the government's commissioner in relation to Knin municipality on the 6th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You had an impression that he came along later. I'm just putting into evidence his appointment here.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, okay. I could well have been mistaken about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The next document, 2D01-0007. Tab 111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D55, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First time of the numbers of James Bond and Nelson come together.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.text: I would say that James Bond and Nelson are admitted into evidence but D55 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were uncertain in your statement or you had a view he may have left very quickly but we see here that he left his appointment on March the 28th, 1996. So after you had left Knin.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Then I was -- let me just verify. This is the commissioner of the government for the town of Knin, which would be the mayor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Then I was mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I just refer to that because of what was in your statement and just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to Mr. Pasic, can we deal with a -- a report from Mr. Al-Alfi, 65 ter 4100, tab 9. Date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not in evidence yet, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Needs a number. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D56, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D56 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's dealings with Mr. Pasic that I'm concerned with. We can see in paragraph 1 that there was a meeting with him, and his description as being in line 4 in charge of the restoration of civilian facilities in Knin. Did you have dealings with him direct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have on one or two occasions, but I don't recall that we dealt with him very much, or that I dealt with him very much if at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it may just be a problem of recollection. I just don't really recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The document that we couldn't find that I wanted to refer to on the 23rd of August, which is a -- a report -- message from Mr. Al-Alfi in fact refers to him intending to go to Plavno on the 25th of August with Mr. Romanic for a meeting with the local people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just seek some verification first before --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm reading in paragraph 1: "This morning I had a meeting with Mr. Pasic, the mayor of Knin. Also present at the meeting were Mr. Djakovic, deputy to the mayor, and Mr. Damir Vidovic, who is in charge of the restoration of civilian facilities in Knin." Now, in your question you suggest that it was Mr. Pasic who was in charge of the restoration of the facilities in Knin, which is not in my knowledge of the English language what I read in line four.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll put my hands up. I was reading very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- would your answer be any different knowing this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think it would. I think I agreed with Mr. Kay that the mayor had responsibility. It appears that the Court is quite right, it was Mr. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In general, I would like -- I appreciate that the parties try to speed up. At the same time, I would also appreciate if the highest precision would be upheld. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect that he was to go to Plavno on that morning of the 25th of August with Mr. Romanic to meet the local population?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember specifically that Mayor Pasic was to be part of that delegation, but there was apparently a meeting set up in Plavno on the 25th of August, and he could well have been a part of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We saw it referred to in the DVD clip on the first day of your evidence. You recollect that the lady said, "But no one came. There was a meeting arranged, but no one came."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. There was also a meeting in the town that we visited first, Zorici, and there were local authorities, as I recall, at that meeting. And I'm not sure that there was any meeting that took place on the other side of the valley, let's say across near Grubori, because I don't believe that those local residents from Grubori found a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It seemed from the terms of her statement in the video, on the film, that she had gone down to what is a local place for a meeting and no one came, so that there was a meeting scheduled.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my impression, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know if in fact that was the meeting that Mr. Romanic was supposed to go to on the 25th and didn't go?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The meeting in Zorici to which you referred, did Mr. Romanic go to that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to recall that. I don't believe he did, but I think there was some discussion of improving the humanitarian situation of the people there, and I think that there was some representation from local authorities, but I'm not sure who that was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We'll need to turn to that document that I was trying to find, Your Honour. I can't deal with this in any other way other than producing the missing document, which is my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dealings with the mayor, you didn't have many, but as we see in D56, the matters of which you were concerned, the humanitarian position of the local population were matters that were discussed with him. And if we look on the second page of D56 exhibit. In paragraph (d): "The mayor also expressed the desire to assist Serbs who left the area during the recent hostilities to come back to their houses." In your dealings with him, was that his position?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the position he expressed in meetings that I was present at, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect that his position was also that such a process for the return of Serbs may be complicated?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that before returning, those who had left would have to apply for Croatian citizenship at the liaison office in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At about that time it was becoming clear that there would be that kind of procedure for people to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. In (f): "It was brought to the attention of the mayor that reports about continuing burning of villages and looting until this time, and he acknowledged that problem and informed Mr. Al-Alfi that the military and civilian authorities are having regular meetings to put an end to such acts." Was that his position in your dealings with him?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he believed crimes were being committed by what was being done unlawfully. Would you accept that position?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, but I'm afraid my memory of discussions with the mayor is a little hazy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. If we go to page 3 of this document, there is a meeting in the afternoon of the report of Mr. Al-Alfi at which you're named as being present.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you provide a separate report in relation to that meeting, or is the information here not in any report submitted by you in evidence?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's the 18th of August, and it's a message, and it starts at paragraph 1, "This morning." So we can take the date as the 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see. This is for the people accommodated inside UNCRO battalion locations to Sector South headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not submit a separate report on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Did you review Mr. Al-Alfi's report or did he just send it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD FLYNN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He must have just sent it. I didn't review it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm looking at the clock. I would need one and a half minutes to find out how we will proceed tomorrow before you start a new line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, looking at the time Your Honour's one and a half minutes is there already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, but you have not gone through the substance of this report. Perhaps it is good that Mr. Flynn stays, because we will speak about tomorrow. Mr. Kay, until now you are close to four hours, which would leave you another hour. What will be the sequence tomorrow? Second in line would be? Mr. Kuzmanovic, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you, as you told us, Mr. Kuzmanovic, you needed two hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, half an hour at the most, if any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half an hour, if any. Mr. Misetic, then I might have mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I may need about two hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest the following: Mr. Kay, tomorrow until 10.00 it's your time even if you would lose a couple of minutes, but I really want to finish tomorrow. Then from 10 to 10.30, Mr. Kuzmanovic, it would be for you. Mr. Misetic, then after the first break usually we have one and a half hour available. If you could try to see whether you could fit that in into that. If not entirely, then you may take another 15 minutes after the break, and then we would have left approximately one hour for re-examination, questions by the Bench, although the Bench of course has put already some questions. Ms. Mahindaratne, part of the exercise of Mr. Kay today has been to -- well, mainly to present a lot of documents. Almost all of these documents not known to the witness, and therefore rather to verify whether this material was available when he gave his statement, and I think in addition to that to inform the Chamber about the existence of such documents. May I take it that it will not -- that you will not need lengthy time in view of the characterisation I just gave from the cross-examination? Could you inform the Chamber what your estimate at this moment would be?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't anticipate too much of time spent on re-examination. It would be a brief, at the most half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That means that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But may I just add, Mr. President, it also depends on what will come out in evidence through cross-examination for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I do understand. These are always commitments under certain reservations. Then I take it that we could finish tomorrow with the examination of Mr. Flynn. At the same time, I don't think that there would be much time left for the next witness to be called, and therefore rather than to have the next witness on standby for almost the whole of the day, then perhaps to just use five or ten minutes we might use that for the MFIs, and then perhaps release the next witness until Monday. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I raise a matter? I have to confess that I was too conservative in my time estimate and that I might need more time. I've been trying to move as quickly as I can with a wide-ranging witness in a way that I felt best dealt with those issues as far as the Defence for Mr. Cermak are concerned. I will, of course, review my materials in the break, and Your Honour has characterised the approach of the Defence to try and more finely tune the remaining issues to deal with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course one of the possibilities would be, but please consider it and please speak about it with Ms. Mahindaratne, that some of the documents as such perhaps could be introduced in by other means than through the witness unless there's any specific reason to assume that the witness could add something to it. There might be other ways of -- I noticed that even before questions were put, the Prosecution often already did not object against admission. To see whether there's anyway of getting this material in evidence, perhaps to make a selection where you would expect the witness to -- to be in a position to further clarify matters in those and where you would expect the witness mainly to say that if he would be aware of this that he might have had to reconsider his opinions. It's clear that this witness gave -- gives his -- his observations, his impressions in a rather clear way and that perhaps it's not for all of the information necessary to say, "Well, if I would have known this, I might not have drawn exactly the same conclusions," because what he tells us what he observed, why he formed certain opinions or gained some impressions, of course an adaptation of that or perhaps I should say make it not as absolute as it sounds on paper up till this moment, of course. The Chamber can do something in that respect as well and say this is what the witness observed. We now have additional information, so that might -- but first perhaps focus on those matters where you would expect the witness to add something on the basis of new information you provide to him. At the same time, I would like to -- I would really like to see whether we can finish tomorrow. I'll also ask Mr. Registrar to see whether there's any margin of perhaps 15 minutes available. That depends on other Chambers. You also may have noticed that -- that where the Prosecution took three hours here in view of the material tendered, the 92 ter, that the Chamber now allowed for close to eight hours, which is of course far more than the 1 to 1, but for good reasons. Nevertheless, I'd like you to discuss both with Ms. Mahindaratne and with other counsel to see -- to find a schedule such that we can finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honours' observations are absolutely understood by us, and we will certainly be working towards that -- that end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I just got something which I have to read before I know whether ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was brought to my attention had been dealt with already. That's the next witness. If there's nothing else, we adjourn until tomorrow, the 11th of April, 9.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
